etymology: From Old Norse skopa "to mock"; appearing throughout the Wisdom literature and Peter's apostolic warning.
biblical_def: To mock with contempt — especially mocking holy things, prophetic warning, or divine judgment; the characteristic posture of the proud heart toward God's word (2 Pet 3:3-4; Prov 1:22).
webster_summary: To mock with contempt, especially of sacred truth.
webster_full: To treat with insolent contempt; to deride; to express contempt by jests or jokes; in Scripture especially the proud heart's mocking of divine warning, prophetic word, and the day of judgment.
scriptures: 2 Peter 3:3-4
There shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts, and saying, Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were.
Proverbs 1:22
How long, ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity? and the scorners delight in their scorning, and fools hate knowledge?
Habakkuk 1:10
And they shall scoff at the kings, and the princes shall be a scorn unto them.
corruption_summary: Glamorized as edgy intellectual independence rather than diagnosed as the proud heart's resistance to truth.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern culture made scoffing a posture of sophistication. Scripture diagnoses it as a moral condition: the heart that has hardened against truth. The scoffer is not smarter than the believer — he is more compromised. Read Proverbs and 2 Peter slowly to see the indictment.
roots_summary: Greek empaiktēs — mocker; Hebrew lits — to scoff.
usage: Beware the scoffer's seat (Psalm 1:1).
Last-days mockery is predicted; do not join it.

etymology: Agent noun from "scoff"; KJV-era English for the Hebrew lits and Greek empaiktēs.
biblical_def: A person whose habitual posture toward truth, authority, and divine warning is contemptuous mockery; a hardened type in Proverbs and a marker of last-days rebellion in 2 Peter.
webster_summary: One who habitually mocks the truth.
webster_full: A person who treats the things of God, His word, His warnings, and His servants with habitual contempt; one who has settled into mockery as a way of life. In Proverbs the scoffer is contrasted with the wise; in 2 Peter he is the marker of the last days.
scriptures: Proverbs 9:7-8
He that reproveth a scorner getteth to himself shame... reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee.
Proverbs 13:1
A wise son heareth his father's instruction: but a scorner heareth not rebuke.
2 Peter 3:3
Knowing this first, that there shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts.
corruption_summary: Romanticized as the brave skeptic; Proverbs paints him as the foolish hardened heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The scoffer is not the smart skeptic — he is the hardened fool. Scripture says he is past correction; reproof only makes him angry. The rebuke is not for the scoffer's benefit (he won't receive it) but to mark him for the wise as someone to be avoided.
usage: Do not waste reproof on a scoffer.
Mark him for what he is and walk on.

etymology: Agent noun from "scorn"; KJV translation of Hebrew lits.
biblical_def: Synonym for scoffer in Proverbs — one whose disposition toward correction is contempt rather than receptivity (Prov 9:7-8; 13:1; 21:24).
webster_summary: One who treats correction with contempt.
webster_full: The KJV synonym for scoffer; one who treats correction, instruction, and the fear of the LORD with proud contempt; the wise are commanded to avoid him for he cannot be helped.
scriptures: Proverbs 21:24
Proud and haughty scorner is his name, who dealeth in proud wrath.
Proverbs 22:10
Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out; yea, strife and reproach shall cease.
Psalm 1:1
Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.
corruption_summary: Mistaken as merely a personality type; Proverbs treats it as a moral category requiring active separation.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs treats the scorner as a contagion, not a quirk. 'Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out.' The wise community has the right and duty to remove the perpetually contemptuous. Tolerance of scorners breeds strife in every direction.
usage: Cast out the scorner; peace returns.
Do not sit in the scorner's seat.

etymology: From Old French moquer "to deride"; widely used in KJV for Hebrew laag and Greek empaizō.
biblical_def: To make sport of, deride, or treat with derisive imitation; in Scripture, the consistent response of the wicked to God's prophets, Christ at the cross, and the truth itself.
webster_summary: To deride, ridicule, treat with derisive imitation.
webster_full: To imitate in contempt or derision; to ridicule; in Scripture, the recurring response of the wicked toward God's prophets, His Son on the cross, and His truth — and a sin God will not let pass: 'Be not deceived; God is not mocked.'
scriptures: Galatians 6:7
Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
Matthew 27:29
And when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head... and they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews!
2 Chronicles 36:16
But they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD arose against his people.
corruption_summary: Treated as mere humor; Scripture treats persistent mockery as the unforgivable line.
corruption_paragraphs: A culture that mocks everything is a culture without holy ground. 2 Chronicles 36:16 says Israel was destroyed because 'they mocked the messengers of God.' Galatians 6:7 says God is not mocked. There is a line where derision becomes judgment-summoning.
roots_summary: Greek empaizō — to mock; Hebrew laag — to deride.
usage: God is not mocked.
Persistent national mockery summons judgment.

etymology: Agent noun from "mock."
biblical_def: One who derides, ridicules, or makes sport of holy things; in Scripture often paired with scoffer and drunkard (Prov 20:1; Isa 28:22).
webster_summary: One who habitually derides, especially holy things.
webster_full: One who habitually derides; in Scripture often paired with the drunkard ('wine is a mocker'), the scoffer, and the proud; a category of the unwise to be avoided and warned against.
scriptures: Proverbs 20:1
Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise.
Isaiah 28:22
Now therefore be ye not mockers, lest your bands be made strong: for I have heard from the Lord GOD of hosts a consumption.
Jude 1:18
How that they told you there should be mockers in the last time, who should walk after their own ungodly lusts.
corruption_summary: Reduced to a mild personality flaw rather than the spiritual marker Scripture makes it.
corruption_paragraphs: Mockery is its own sin. Both wine and the wicked heart act as mockers — they distort sense and sound until truth seems funny. The cure is sobriety: of mind, of spirit, of speech. Be slow to mock; quick to repent of mocking.
usage: Wine is a mocker; so is the proud heart.
Last-days mockers are predicted.

etymology: From Latin deridere "to mock to scorn," de- + ridere "to laugh."
biblical_def: Mocking laughter; the contemptuous response of the wicked to the godly, and conversely, the LORD's response to those who plot against His Christ (Ps 2:4; 22:7; 44:13).
webster_summary: Mocking laughter; contemptuous ridicule.
webster_full: The act of laughing in scorn; contemptuous ridicule; in Scripture both the suffering of the godly under wicked mockery and the divine response of the One who sits in the heavens and holds rebellious kings in derision.
scriptures: Psalm 2:4
He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision.
Psalm 22:7
All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head.
Jeremiah 20:7
I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me.
corruption_summary: Reduced to weather of culture rather than recognized as the suffering of the prophet and the prophet's response in God.
corruption_paragraphs: Derision is what the godly bear from the world (Ps 22:7) and what God lays on the proud (Ps 2:4). Christ at the cross was the climax of human derision; the One who sat in the heavens was holding all of it in His own greater derision. Derision is bilingual.
usage: Bear derision as Christ did.
God holds rebels in derision.

etymology: From Latin ridiculum "that which excites laughter," from ridere "to laugh."
biblical_def: Mockery employing humor to belittle; the device of Sanballat against Nehemiah's wall, of Israel's enemies against the prophets, and of the world against Christ's people (Neh 4:1-3; Heb 11:36).
webster_summary: Mockery employing humor to belittle.
webster_full: Words or actions intended to provoke contemptuous laughter at a person or idea; in Scripture often the first weapon of the enemy when direct opposition is too costly — Sanballat ridiculed before Tobiah attacked, Job's mockers laughed before they accused.
scriptures: Nehemiah 4:1-2
When Sanballat heard that we builded the wall, he was wroth... and mocked the Jews. And he spake before his brethren and the army of Samaria, and said, What do these feeble Jews?
Hebrews 11:36
And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment.
Acts 17:32
When they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter.
corruption_summary: Treated as harmless wit; Scripture treats it as a weapon often deployed against godly work.
corruption_paragraphs: Ridicule is the world's standing weapon against gospel work. Athenian philosophers ridiculed resurrection; Sanballat ridiculed wall-building; the cross-watchers ridiculed the Crucified. Expect ridicule; do not be derailed by it. Build anyway. Speak anyway. Trust anyway.
usage: Expect ridicule; build anyway.
Sanballat mocked first; opposed second.

etymology: From Old French geste "deed, exploit"; later "jocular tale," then any joking.
biblical_def: Joking, especially the kind that is improper for saints — coarse, crude, or making sport of holy things (Eph 5:4; Prov 26:18-19).
webster_summary: Joking, especially improper or coarse joking.
webster_full: Words spoken in mirth or play; especially the foolish talking and coarse jesting Paul rules out of place among saints (Eph 5:4) and the dangerous jesting of Proverbs 26 — 'Am I not in sport?' — by which a man hides destruction under a joke.
scriptures: Ephesians 5:4
Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks.
Proverbs 26:18-19
As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am I not in sport?
Ecclesiastes 7:6
For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool.
corruption_summary: Defended as harmless fun, missing how Paul lists it among character violations of saintly speech.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul does not condemn humor; he condemns 'jesting' — the coarse, double-meaning, sacred-belittling kind. The man who jests about everything has no holy ground left. Recover the distinction between cheerful holy laughter and the corrosive jest.
usage: Be cheerful; not coarsely jesting.
Holy laughter is not corrosive jest.

etymology: From Middle French tanter "to provoke," the prophets' word for ridiculing oracle.
biblical_def: A song or speech of bitter mockery, especially the prophetic taunt-song against fallen kings and nations (Isa 14; Hab 2:6; Mic 2:4).
webster_summary: A bitter mocking speech, especially prophetic against the fallen.
webster_full: A speech or song of bitter mockery; the prophets compose extended taunt-songs against fallen Babylon (Isa 14), Tyre (Ezek 27), and the proud rich (Hab 2). The form is divinely sanctioned poetic mockery of evil judged.
scriptures: Isaiah 14:4
Thou shalt take up this proverb (taunt) against the king of Babylon, and say, How hath the oppressor ceased! the golden city ceased!
Habakkuk 2:6
Shall not all these take up a parable against him, and a taunting proverb against him.
Micah 2:4
In that day shall one take up a parable against you, and lament with a doleful lamentation.
corruption_summary: Confused with personal insult; Scripture's taunt is a prophetic genre against systemic evil.
corruption_paragraphs: The biblical taunt is corporate and prophetic, not personal. The prophet sings a taunt over the fallen tyrant after God has judged him. It is not playground mockery; it is canonical mocking-poetry of evil broken.
usage: Read Isaiah 14 as a taunt-song over Babylon.
Prophetic taunt is canonical.

etymology: Likely from Dutch gieren "to roar"; later "to mock with shouts."
biblical_def: To mock with raucous shouting; the noisy mocking of crowds — at the cross, against Jeremiah, against Elisha (Mark 15:29-32; Jer 20:7-8; 2 Kings 2:23).
webster_summary: To mock with noisy crowd-shouting.
webster_full: To mock loudly, often in groups; the crowd-shouting form of mockery seen in the soldiers and passers-by at Calvary, in the small boys against Elisha, and in the persecutors of Jeremiah.
scriptures: And they that passed by railed on him, wagging their heads, and saying, Ah, thou that destroyest the temple, and buildest it in three days, Save thyself.
2 Kings 2:23
There came forth little children out of the city, and mocked him, and said unto him, Go up, thou bald head; go up, thou bald head.
Jeremiah 20:7
I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me.
corruption_summary: Trivialized as crowd-noise; Scripture takes the public derision of God's servants extremely seriously.
corruption_paragraphs: The 42 small boys mauled by bears for jeering Elisha sounds harsh until you realize: they were not children but a young mob, mocking a prophet at Bethel, the seat of golden-calf idolatry. God takes public mockery of His servants with deadly seriousness.
usage: Crowd-jeers test the messenger.
Christ at Calvary bore them silently.

etymology: From Old English fnǣran "to snort," extended to silent contempt.
biblical_def: Silent or near-silent expression of contempt — facial mockery; characteristic of Pharisaic response to Christ's teaching on money (Luke 16:14).
webster_summary: Silent facial expression of contempt.
webster_full: The often-silent expression of contempt by curling the lip or twisting the face; in the gospels the Pharisees 'derided' Jesus over His teaching on money, the Greek word literally meaning 'to turn up the nose.' A sneer can communicate without sound.
scriptures: Luke 16:14
And the Pharisees also, who were covetous, heard all these things: and they derided him.
Psalm 22:7
All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head.
They have gaped upon me with their mouth; they have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully.
corruption_summary: Read as innocuous body-language; Scripture treats facial contempt as a marker of the heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The sneer is the heart's leak. Pharisees who could not refute Jesus sneered at Him. Job's accusers gaped before they spoke. Watch the face before the words; the heart shows itself there. And watch your own face — the sneer betrays.
roots_summary: Greek ekmyktērizō — to turn up the nose.
usage: Watch the face for the heart's leak.
The sneer betrays before the words.

etymology: From Middle English gain (against) + say — "one who speaks against."
biblical_def: A KJV term for one who contradicts or opposes — particularly a teacher who must be silenced for distorting sound doctrine (Titus 1:9; Rom 10:21).
webster_summary: One who contradicts; an obstinate opposer of truth.
webster_full: The KJV term for one who speaks against (Greek antilegō) — a contradicter or opponent; in the pastoral epistles a category of false teachers whom the elder must be able to convince and silence by sound doctrine.
scriptures: Titus 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Romans 10:21
All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people.
Jude 1:11
Woe unto them! for... they... perished in the gainsaying of Core.
corruption_summary: Forgotten KJV vocabulary; the role of the elder to silence gainsayers is largely lost in modern church culture.
corruption_paragraphs: Titus 1:9 makes refuting gainsayers a qualification for elders. Modern church culture often treats doctrinal correction as unloving, leaving gainsayers free to mislead. Sound doctrine confronts opposing voices; the elder is built for it.
usage: Elders refute gainsayers.
Sound doctrine quiets opposing voices.

etymology: From Old French railler "to mock"; KJV term for a verbal abuser.
biblical_def: One given to abusive, slanderous, mocking speech; listed by Paul as a category of brother to be excluded from fellowship (1 Cor 5:11; cf. 'reviler').
webster_summary: One who uses abusive mocking speech.
webster_full: The KJV term for an abusive, slanderous, mocking speaker; in Paul's list of those a so-called brother must not be to remain in fellowship — alongside fornicator, idolater, drunkard, extortioner — railers are excluded from table-fellowship for their tongue-sin.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 5:11
If any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat.
1 Peter 3:9
Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing.
1 Corinthians 6:10
Nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: Tongue-sin gets de-prioritized below 'real' sins; Paul refuses to let it.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul lists the railer with the fornicator and idolater. Christian culture often treats verbal abuse as less serious than sexual sin or theft — Paul does not. The railer's tongue can ruin a body of believers as thoroughly as any other sin. Discipline accordingly.
usage: Tongue-sin is in Paul's exclusion list.
Bless when railed against; do not return.

etymology: From Latin re- + vilis (worthless) — "to speak as worthless."
biblical_def: One who speaks abusively, attacks character, and dishonors with the tongue; excluded from inheriting the kingdom (1 Cor 6:10) and barred from communion (1 Cor 5:11).
webster_summary: An abusive verbal attacker.
webster_full: One who attacks character and reputation with abusive speech; another rendering of Greek loidoros — alongside railer; named in Paul's lists of those who shall not inherit the kingdom and those a so-called brother must not be.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 6:10
Nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God.
1 Peter 2:23
Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously.
1 Timothy 5:14
I will therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house, give none occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully.
corruption_summary: Treated as venting or 'speaking truth'; Scripture knows abusive speech for what it is and bars it.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ was reviled and did not revile back (1 Pet 2:23) — the deepest answer to a reviler is silence and trust in God's judgment. Vengeance with the tongue is still vengeance. The Christ-pattern is to entrust the matter to the Judge.
usage: Christ was reviled and did not revile back.
Entrust verbal harm to the Judge.

etymology: Greek blasphēmos — "speaking injuriously," especially of sacred things.
biblical_def: One who speaks contemptuously of God or holy things; a serious category of sin Paul confessed himself to have been before conversion (1 Tim 1:13; cf. Rev 13:5).
webster_summary: One who speaks contemptuously of God or holy things.
webster_full: One who speaks injuriously of God or holy things; a category Paul applies to himself before conversion ('a blasphemer, a persecutor, and injurious'); also applied to the eschatological beast and false prophet who speak great things against the Most High.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 1:13
Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.
Revelation 13:5
And there was given unto him a mouth speaking great things and blasphemies.
All sins shall be forgiven... but he that shall blaspheme against the Holy Ghost hath never forgiveness.
corruption_summary: Reduced to taking God's name in vain (which it includes) but Scripture's category is broader — speaking against God's character or work.
corruption_paragraphs: Blasphemy is wider than profanity. Paul calls his pre-conversion zeal blasphemy because he attacked Christ in attacking the church. Whoever speaks against the work of God in the name of God can be a blasphemer of the Spirit. Tread carefully near holy things.
usage: Paul: I was a blasphemer; I obtained mercy.
The unforgivable sin is against the Spirit.

etymology: From Latin impudens — "shameless."
biblical_def: Shameless; without proper shame in the face of holy reproof — the disposition Ezekiel was sent to speak to (Ezek 2:4; 3:7).
webster_summary: Shameless; without proper sense of shame.
webster_full: Shameless; without proper sense of shame in the face of holy reproof; the prevailing disposition of Israel to whom God sent Ezekiel — a hard-faced, hard-hearted, hard-forehead house unwilling to receive correction.
scriptures: Ezekiel 2:4
For they are impudent children and stiffhearted. I do send thee unto them; and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD.
Ezekiel 3:7
But the house of Israel will not hearken unto thee... for all the house of Israel are impudent and hardhearted.
Proverbs 7:13
So she caught him, and kissed him, and with an impudent face said unto him...
corruption_summary: Praised as boldness or confidence; Scripture sees shamelessness as moral catastrophe.
corruption_paragraphs: A culture without shame is in serious trouble. Shame is the soul's smoke detector — when it stops working, fires burn unaccounted. Ezekiel's hearers had impudent foreheads; God sent him anyway, knowing they would not hear. Sometimes the prophet preaches to leave the verdict standing.
usage: Pray for the gift of holy shame.
Beware praising shamelessness as bravery.

etymology: From Latin insolens — "unaccustomed, immoderate, arrogant."
biblical_def: Arrogantly disrespectful; the bearing of those who treat sacred things with brash contempt; characteristic of those Paul lists in the Romans 1 indictment (Rom 1:30, ESV).
webster_summary: Arrogantly disrespectful; brashly contemptuous.
webster_full: Arrogantly disrespectful; insulting in manner or speech; characteristic of the proud heart that treats sacred things, lawful authority, and one's elders with brash contempt; named in Paul's catalog of unrighteousness in Romans 1.
scriptures: Romans 1:30
Backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents.
1 Timothy 1:13
Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious.
Proverbs 21:24
Proud and haughty scorner is his name, who dealeth in proud wrath.
corruption_summary: Mistaken for confidence or wit; Scripture lists it among the markers of unrighteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's word in 1 Timothy 1:13 (KJV 'injurious') is the same root that gives us 'insolent' in modern English. Insolence is not boldness — it is the arrogant heart breaking out at the mouth. Paul's testimony: he was insolent before mercy met him.
usage: Insolence is hubris with a tongue.
Repent of it before God's mercy meets you.

etymology: From Latin arrogare — "to claim for oneself."
biblical_def: Claiming more for oneself than is one's due; the heart-disposition God resists (James 4:6); a marker of last-days behavior (2 Tim 3:2).
webster_summary: Claiming more than one's due; God-resisted.
webster_full: Claiming more for oneself than is rightful; an exalted opinion of one's own qualities or rights; the disposition God 'resists' (James 4:6) and which characterizes last-days perilous times (2 Tim 3:2).
scriptures: James 4:6
But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.
2 Timothy 3:2
For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy.
Proverbs 8:13
The fear of the LORD is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate.
corruption_summary: Reframed as confidence or self-esteem; Scripture maintains the verdict — God resists it.
corruption_paragraphs: The age tells you to believe in yourself; Scripture says God resists those who do. Confidence in Christ is humility; confidence in self is arrogance. Recover the difference. The proud heart will be humbled — better now than at the judgment.
roots_summary: Latin arrogare — to claim for oneself.
usage: God resists the proud; humble yourself.
Self-esteem is not the gospel.

etymology: From Old French haut "high."
biblical_def: High-and-mighty; exalting oneself above others; the disposition Scripture pairs with destruction (Prov 16:18) and which the LORD specifically opposes (Isa 2:11).
webster_summary: Lifted-up in spirit; high-and-mighty toward others.
webster_full: Lifted up in spirit; treating others as beneath; the bearing Scripture pairs with destruction in Proverbs 16:18, with the day of the LORD's judgment in Isaiah 2:11, and with God's specific resistance throughout the wisdom literature.
scriptures: Proverbs 16:18
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
Isaiah 2:11
The lofty looks of man shall be humbled, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day.
Isaiah 2:17
The loftiness of man shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men shall be made low.
corruption_summary: Confused with strength or composure; Scripture isolates haughtiness as a target of judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 2 announces a day when haughtiness will be specifically humbled. The same God who lifts the lowly bows the high. Pre-empt the day; humble yourself now. The fall is sure for haughty hearts; the rescue is for the broken-and-contrite.
usage: Haughty spirits go before falls.
The Day humbles the lofty look.

etymology: From Latin praesumere — "to take before, take for granted."
biblical_def: Acting boldly without warrant; the high-handed sin distinguished from sins of weakness in the Mosaic law (Num 15:30-31); the prayer of David: 'keep back thy servant from presumptuous sins' (Ps 19:13).
webster_summary: Acting boldly without warrant; the high-handed sin.
webster_full: Acting boldly without warrant or right; in Mosaic law, the 'high-handed' sin done deliberately and defiantly, distinguished from sins of weakness or ignorance and not covered by the regular sacrifices; David prays for protection from such sins in Psalm 19:13.
scriptures: Numbers 15:30
But the soul that doeth ought presumptuously, whether he be born in the land, or a stranger, the same reproacheth the LORD.
Psalm 19:13
Keep back thy servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me: then shall I be upright, and I shall be innocent from the great transgression.
2 Peter 2:10
But chiefly them that walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness, and despise government. Presumptuous are they, selfwilled, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities.
corruption_summary: Confused with confidence; Scripture distinguishes presumption (acting without God) from faith (acting with God).
corruption_paragraphs: Faith and presumption look alike to the casual eye. Both step out boldly. The difference: faith goes where God has clearly sent; presumption goes where He has not. David prays daily protection from presumption. So should we.
usage: Pray Psalm 19:13 daily.
Faith goes where God sends; presumption where He has not.

etymology: Hebrew kesil / nabal / evil — three different fool-words in Proverbs.
biblical_def: Not the comic figure but the morally rebellious — the one who has said in his heart, 'There is no God' (Ps 14:1); the one who hates knowledge (Prov 1:22) and despises correction.
webster_summary: The morally rebellious heart that rejects God and correction.
webster_full: The biblical fool is moral, not intellectual. Hebrew has multiple terms: kesil (dull-stubborn), nabal (morally bankrupt), evil (perverse). All denote the heart that rejects God, hates correction, and persists in self-rule. Closely related to the scoffer.
scriptures: Psalm 14:1
The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works.
Proverbs 1:7
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
Proverbs 26:11
As a dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly.
corruption_summary: Reduced to comic figure; Scripture's fool is a moral indictment, not an entertainer.
corruption_paragraphs: The biblical fool is not a court jester — he is a moral category. He says God isn't there; he despises wisdom; he returns to his folly. The wise community is to recognize foolishness for what it is and not entrust authority to it.
usage: The biblical fool is a moral category.
Read Proverbs to recognize him.

etymology: Opening psalm of the Psalter, framing the whole book as the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked.
biblical_def: The opening psalm contrasting the blessed man (who delights in God's law) with the ungodly (who walk in counsel of the wicked, stand in the way of sinners, sit in the seat of the scornful).
webster_summary: The opening psalm of the two ways.
webster_full: The first psalm of the Psalter, framing the entire book as a choice between two ways: the blessed man who delights in God's law and is like a tree planted by waters, and the ungodly who are chaff that the wind drives away.
scriptures: Psalm 1:1
Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.
Psalm 1:2
But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
Psalm 1:6
For the LORD knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish.
corruption_summary: Read as gentle pastoral; missing how it sets up the entire Psalter as moral confrontation.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 1 is a doorway. Walk through and the rest of the Psalter holds the two ways together. Notice the descent in v1: walk → stand → sit. From wicked counsel, to sinful association, to the scornful seat. Folly nests, then settles.
usage: Read Psalm 1 as the doorway to the Psalter.
Watch the descent: walk, stand, sit.

etymology: From Old English fra-weard — "turned away," opposite of toward.
biblical_def: Perverse; turned-away from what is right; the KJV's word for the crooked-hearted person whose mouth, ways, and thoughts have all gone the wrong direction (Prov 4:24; 6:12; 11:20).
webster_summary: Perverse; turned away from rightness.
webster_full: The KJV adjective for those whose nature has turned away from rightness — froward mouth, froward heart, froward generation. The opposite is upright. Contemporary English has lost the word; the moral category survives.
scriptures: Proverbs 4:24
Put away from thee a froward mouth, and perverse lips put far from thee.
Proverbs 6:12
A naughty person, a wicked man, walketh with a froward mouth.
Proverbs 11:20
They that are of a froward heart are abomination to the LORD: but such as are upright in their way are his delight.
corruption_summary: Vocabulary fallen out of use; the moral perception it captured is fading too.
corruption_paragraphs: When a culture loses a word, it often loses the perception that word served. 'Froward' captured a real moral state: the heart that has turned. Modern English speaks of 'crooked' or 'twisted'; the older word held the directional sense — turned away. Recover the perception.
usage: Read Proverbs in KJV to recover the word.
Froward hearts grieve God.

etymology: Hebrew metaphor from oxen who refuse the yoke; used repeatedly of Israel.
biblical_def: Stubbornly refusing instruction or correction; the figure drawn from oxen that will not bend the neck to the yoke; God's repeated diagnosis of Israel (Exod 32:9; 33:3; 34:9; Acts 7:51).
webster_summary: Stubbornly refusing the yoke of God.
webster_full: The metaphor drawn from yoke-resistant oxen — stubbornly refusing instruction, correction, or covenant; God's repeated diagnosis of Israel from Sinai onward, brought to climax in Stephen's indictment of his hearers in Acts 7:51.
scriptures: Exodus 32:9
And the LORD said unto Moses, I have seen this people, and, behold, it is a stiffnecked people.
Acts 7:51
Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye.
Deuteronomy 9:6
For thou art a stiffnecked people.
corruption_summary: Treated as an obscure idiom; missing how thoroughly it encapsulates the human heart's refusal of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Every nation goes stiff-necked. Israel did; we do. The cure is not lecturing the neck but receiving the yoke that is easy and the burden that is light. Christ offers exchange: come unto Me and I will give you rest. Stiff necks unbend at the cross.
usage: Stiff necks unbend only at the cross.
Christ's yoke is the cure.

etymology: From Old French rebucher — "to beat back."
biblical_def: Pointed verbal correction of error or sin, commanded as part of the gospel ministry (2 Tim 4:2); to be received by the wise (Prov 9:8) and refused by the scorner.
webster_summary: Pointed verbal correction; gospel-ministry command.
webster_full: Pointed verbal correction of sin or error; commanded by Paul as part of the gospel ministry alongside reproof and exhortation; received gladly by the wise (Prov 9:8) and rejected by the scorner; refused at the cost of one's soul.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 4:2
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Proverbs 9:8
Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee.
Proverbs 27:5
Open rebuke is better than secret love.
corruption_summary: Avoided as unloving in modern church culture; Scripture commands it as part of love.
corruption_paragraphs: The age treats correction as cruelty. Paul commands it as ministry. Proverbs says open rebuke is better than secret love — silence about sin is not kindness, it is abandonment. Learn to rebuke; learn to receive rebuke. Both are gospel skills.
roots_summary: Hebrew yakach — to reprove; Greek epitimaō — to rebuke.
usage: Open rebuke is better than secret love.
Rebuke the wise; they love you for it.

etymology: English negation of 'teachable'; concept appears throughout Proverbs as the fool's marker.
biblical_def: Refusing instruction; the heart that will not be corrected; the marker of the fool, the scoffer, and the stiff-necked (Prov 12:1; 15:5; Hos 4:6).
webster_summary: Refusing instruction; the fool's marker.
webster_full: The disposition that refuses to be taught — by parents, mentors, Scripture, or the Spirit; named in Proverbs as the marker of the fool ('he that hateth reproof is brutish'); the deepest foundation of every other folly.
scriptures: Proverbs 12:1
Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish.
Proverbs 15:5
A fool despiseth his father's instruction: but he that regardeth reproof is prudent.
Hosea 4:6
My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge.
corruption_summary: Defended as 'thinking for myself'; Scripture diagnoses it as the heart's refusal of life.
corruption_paragraphs: The unteachable heart hates knowledge — and that hatred destroys. Hosea names it as the cause of national ruin. Recover teachability as a virtue: humble hearing, slow speaking, willingness to be wrong. Without it no other wisdom develops.
roots_summary: Hebrew musar — instruction; Greek paideuō — to instruct.
usage: Cultivate teachability as a virtue.
The unteachable heart starves itself.
